name: Factors Affecting the Rate of Photosynthesis
what: Covers the four factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis (light availability, water availability, temperature and CO2 concentration), the concept of a limiting factor, photorespiration and the adaptations of C3, C4 and CAM plants.
why: Understanding how external conditions alter photosynthetic rate requires integrating enzyme theory with the specific biochemistry of photosynthesis. These concepts also connect directly to agricultural applications and are a source of multi-part exam questions.

items.title: I can list the factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis
items.what: The four factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis are light availability, water availability, temperature and carbon dioxide concentration. Each is a limiting factor when in short supply.
items.why: Listing these factors is the starting point for deeper explanation questions. A limiting factor is any factor that slows the rate of photosynthesis when insufficient.
items.example: In a greenhouse at night with artificial lights, light is no longer limiting, but CO2 concentration may become the factor that limits the rate of photosynthesis.

items.title: I can explain why and how each factor affects the rate of photosynthesis
items.what: Light intensity increases reaction rate up to a plateau where chloroplasts are working at maximum capacity. Temperature affects enzyme activity, increasing rate to the optimum then decreasing as enzymes denature. CO2 concentration increases rate until enzyme active sites are saturated. Water stress causes stomata to close, limiting CO2 entry and reducing photosynthesis.
items.why: Examiners regularly ask students to explain the mechanism behind a graph or trend. Knowing the enzyme-based reason for each pattern is required for full marks.
items.example: At temperatures above the optimum, Rubisco denatures and its active site changes shape, so CO2 can no longer bind and carbon fixation stops, causing the rate of photosynthesis to fall sharply.

items.title: I can describe the role of Rubisco in maximising photosynthetic efficiency and define photorespiration
items.what: Rubisco normally fixes CO2 to RuBP to begin the Calvin Cycle. However, when O2 concentration is high (e.g. when stomata are closed), Rubisco binds O2 instead of CO2, initiating photorespiration. Photorespiration is an inefficient process that produces no glucose and wastes energy, reducing photosynthetic efficiency by approximately 25% in C3 plants.
items.why: Photorespiration is a key reason why C3 plants are less efficient in hot, dry conditions and is the basis for understanding why C4 and CAM adaptations are advantageous.
items.example: On a hot dry day, a wheat plant closes its stomata to conserve water. O2 builds up inside the leaf. Rubisco begins binding O2 instead of CO2, and photorespiration occurs, wasting energy and producing no glucose.

items.title: I can summarise the adaptations of C3, C4 and CAM plants that maximise photosynthetic efficiency
items.what: C3 plants (e.g. wheat, rice) fix CO2 directly in the mesophyll using Rubisco but are vulnerable to photorespiration. C4 plants (e.g. maize, sugar cane) fix CO2 as a 4C compound in the mesophyll and release it in low-O2 bundle sheath cells for the Calvin Cycle, reducing photorespiration. CAM plants (e.g. cacti, pineapple) open stomata only at night to fix CO2 as a 4C compound, releasing it during the day when stomata are closed.
items.why: The contrast between C3, C4 and CAM plants is a direct Study Design dot point and often appears as a table-completion or extended response question in exams.
items.example: A CAM plant such as a cactus in a desert opens its stomata at night to take in CO2 and stores it as a 4C compound. During the hot day, stomata remain closed to prevent water loss, and the stored CO2 is released for use in the Calvin Cycle.

items.title: I can draw, recognise and interpret graphical representations of rates of photosynthesis
items.what: Rate of photosynthesis graphs typically show an initial increase with increasing light, CO2 or temperature, followed by a plateau (for light and CO2) or a sharp drop after the optimum (for temperature). Interpreting these graphs requires linking the shape of the curve to enzyme or chloroplast behaviour.
items.why: Graph interpretation is a core scientific skill assessed in both SACs and the external exam. Being able to read off data points and explain the trend using biological reasoning is expected.
items.example: In a graph showing rate of photosynthesis vs light intensity, the flat section of the curve indicates that light is no longer the limiting factor and another factor, such as CO2 concentration or chloroplast capacity, is now limiting the rate.
